Chapter 1 · The question

The work is done. So where is the money?

The grass is cut. The locks are changed. The pipes are safe for winter. The photos are beautiful. And still — tell me — where is the money? Work done is not money earned. Money has to travel, and it leaks at every step.

Before the story begins, say three words from Class 8 from memory: identify, document, quantify. Those three words are about to decide whether our house gets paid.

Say her name first

She was named once, in Class 1, and she is never named again. Her name is on her file at all three desks today. Pick the name your class gave her, or type it in.

That's her — the 1972 house. Same house, ninth chapter. Today we follow her money.
Say it in class

“Work done is not money earned. Money has to travel — and it leaks at every step.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Most people new to this work think the story ends when the crew drives away. It doesn't. The crew's work creates a claim — an amount we ask the client to pay. Between asking and receiving sit a rulebook, an approval, a bill, and a bank. Money can shrink at every one of those stops, for reasons that have nothing to do with how hard anyone worked in the yard.

How to run the opener, step by step

  1. Ask the question cold: “The work is done — where is the money?” Take every guess.
  2. Ask for Class 8's three words from memory: identify, document, quantify.
  3. Then give the carrying sentence (above) and say it once, slowly.
  4. Promise the shape of the day: one staircase, three people, one invoice, six reason codes.

If you've done this work before

You have lived the gap this slide names: a perfect job that paid short, or late, or under a different order number entirely. That gap is not bad luck — it is a set of named leaks, each with an owner. Today the class learns to name them before they happen to them.

The line to remember: “Work done is not money earned.”

The proof — what this class stands on

Everything money-shaped in this class is a synthetic teaching example, labelled as such — a made-up $1,000 invoice, made-up leaks, round numbers chosen so the class can follow them on their fingers. The rules underneath are the programme's standing rules: the rulebook on the order governs, gross equals net on these orders (always check the order), payment lag is about sixty days, and losses always carry a reason code. No real job, amount, or client appears anywhere.

If this is all new to you

In Class 8 you learned to read a house: identify what is wrong, document it with proof, quantify it with honest numbers. Money follows the same three words in the same order. Work you identified but never documented cannot be proved. Work documented but never quantified cannot be priced. Skip a word and the dollar leaks — you will watch it happen on the staircase.

How it happened, step by step

  1. Class 8: the skill on the house — damage read in order.
  2. Class 9: the same skill on the file — the house's story becomes a bid.
  3. Every leak today traces back to one of the three words done badly or skipped.

If you've done this work before

Hold this line for the Processor chapter: a missing photo is not a paperwork problem, it is an identify-document-quantify break — and it is priced, in dollars, on the very first step of the staircase.

The line to remember: “First you identify, then you document, then you quantify — in that order, every time.”

The proof — where the three words sit

The three words are Class 8's assessment skill, carried forward unchanged. This class does not re-teach them; it spends them. If the class cannot say them cold, spend two minutes there — the staircase will not make sense without them.

Chapter 2 · Where the dollar is born

A bid is scope plus rate plus evidence.

Before the dollar starts walking, learn how it is born. Scope — what the order actually asks for, read word by word. Rate — the price the governing rulebook allows for that work. Evidence — the photos and the report that prove the work happened. If any one of the three is missing, there is no bid. That rule never bends.

The rulebook is always the one on the order — never another client's rules, never what we remember from last time.

Say it in class

“The rulebook on the order is the boss. If the rulebook does not allow it, we do not bill it.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Picture a three-legged stool. Scope without rate is work with no honest price. Rate without scope is a price for work nobody asked for. Scope and rate without evidence is a story nobody can check — and uncheckable work does not get paid. A bid only stands when all three legs touch the ground at once.

How a bid is built, step by step

  1. Read the order word by word — that is the scope, nothing added, nothing assumed.
  2. Find each item's price in that order's own rulebook — that is the rate.
  3. Attach the field proof — photos and report — that is the evidence.
  4. Only then write the number. The bid is the three together, never the number alone.

If you've done this work before

Most billing pain you have seen is a missing leg wearing a disguise: the crew did extra work the order never listed (no scope), priced from memory of another client (wrong rate), or photographed so dark nobody could verify it (no evidence). Name the missing leg out loud and the fix is usually obvious.

The line to remember: “Scope plus rate plus evidence equals a bid.”

The proof — the words, pinned down

ScopeWhat the order asks for — read word by word
RateWhat that order's rulebook allows for it
EvidencePhotos + report proving it happened

Definitions as taught in the programme's Session 9. “Governing rulebook” always means the rulebook attached to that one order.

If this is all new to you

Every order arrives with its own set of rules: what may be billed, at what price, with what proof, whether photos need a date printed on them. Two houses on the same street can carry two different rulebooks. The habit that protects you is boring and total: check the order in front of you, every time, even when you are sure you know.

How the trap works, step by step

  1. A trainee learns one client's rules well — a good thing.
  2. The next order comes from a different rulebook, but looks similar.
  3. The remembered rule gets applied — and it is wrong for this order.
  4. The line is cut at review, and the leak gets blamed on “the client.” It wasn't the client. It was the borrowed rulebook.

If you've done this work before

You will hear this again at the date-stamp check and again at gross-equals-net: both are order-specific rules, true on these orders, never to be assumed on the next. Teach the checking habit, not just today's answers.

The line to remember: “Always check the order — this rule is order-specific.”

The proof — provenance, stated plainly

The rulebook-on-the-order rule is one of the programme's standing rules, stated in the blueprint's standing-rules section — an operating rule of this work, taught as such, not a finding from housing history.

Chapter 3 · One dollar walks down

Five steps. Every step leaks. Every leak has an owner.

Imagine one dollar our house has earned, walking down a staircase with five steps: Claimed, Allowable, Approved, Invoiced, Paid. Here is the whole walk on one synthetic invoice of $1,000 — labelled, made up, and chosen round so you can follow it on your fingers.

$1,000ClaimedWhat we ask the client to pay
$800AllowableWhat the order's own rulebook allows us to ask for− $200
$700ApprovedWhat the client agrees to pay− $100
$700InvoicedWhat we actually write on the bill$0 — hold this step in your memory
$550PaidWhat finally arrives in the bank− $150
Say it in class

“Claimed one thousand, allowable eight hundred, approved seven hundred, invoiced seven hundred, paid five hundred and fifty. Every leak has a name, and every leak has an owner. That is the whole money lesson in one staircase.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

The shock of this slide is the point: the crew did $1,000 of claimed work and the bank received $550 — and nobody stole anything. Each gap is a rule doing its job: the rulebook refusing what it never allowed, the client refusing what was never approved in advance, the review refusing what was never proved. Once you can name a gap, you can stop the next one.

How to teach the ladder, step by step

  1. Walk down slowly, one rung at a time. Name the step before you name the number.
  2. At each leak, ask “whose desk is this?” before you answer it yourself.
  3. Say the full ladder aloud, end to end, twice. The class says it the second time.
  4. Flag the honest limit: this ladder is the synthetic claimed-to-paid invoice — it is not the contractor-chain funnel from earlier sessions. Different staircase, different lesson.

If you've done this work before

Notice where the biggest leak sits: the very first step, before the client is involved at all. The $200 was lost at home — unallowable lines and unprovable work that a good check catches before the file ever moves. That is why the Processor's desk, later today, carries the moral centre of the whole job.

The line to remember: “Every leak has a name, and every leak has an owner.”

The proof — the arithmetic, all of it

$1,000 → $800−$200 at Allowable (next slide)
$800 → $700−$100 at Approved (next slide)
$700 → $700$0 at Invoiced (Slide 5)
$700 → $550−$150 at Paid (Slide 5)

Synthetic invoice from the programme's Session 9, labelled as made up wherever it appears. The rung definitions are the session's own.

If this is all new to you

“Owner” here doesn't mean blame — it means the desk where the leak could have been stopped. The $200 allowability leak belongs to the Processor's check. The $100 approval leak belongs to the Vendor Manager's bid step. The $150 paid leak sits on the Client Manager's ground. When a loss has an owner, it has a next action. When it has no owner, it just happens again.

How the ownership map is drawn, step by step

  1. Leak 1 (Claimed → Allowable): the Processor's allowability and proof check.
  2. Leak 2 (Allowable → Approved): the Vendor Manager's bid/approval step.
  3. Leak 3 (Approved → Invoiced): nobody — $0, and worth celebrating.
  4. Leak 4 (Invoiced → Paid): the Client Manager's tracking and fixing.

If you've done this work before

This map is the session in miniature: the next five slides simply walk the three desks in order. If a trainee ever asks “why do we need three roles for one file?” — point at the staircase. Each role exists because one of these leaks exists.

The line to remember: “A loss with an owner has a next action.”

The proof — where the owners come from

The owner assignments are Session 9's own, stated rung by rung in the story: Processor for the first leak, the Vendor Manager's bid/approval step for the second, the Client Manager for the last. The three roles are then taught one desk at a time on Slides 6–8.

Chapter 4 · Leaks one and two

$200 to the rulebook. $100 to not asking first.

First step down: of the $200 lost between Claimed and Allowable, $120 was work the rulebook never allows — hauling away personal things the order never listed. The other $80 was work we probably did but could not prove — photos missing, or too dark to read. Then $100 more fell at Approved, because nobody asked permission before doing work above the allowance.

Unallowable means outside the rulebook — and no rulebook pays for it. Work without proof is work the rulebook cannot pay for either.

Say it in class

“A gap in proof is not a small thing. A gap sends the file back to the field — never paper it over.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Keep the two halves apart, because their fixes are opposite. The $120 (say, removing personal property the order never covered) should never have been billed at all — the fix is to not claim it. The $80 was probably real work — the fix is proof: clear photos, taken properly, tagged to the line they prove. One half is “don't ask,” the other is “show me.” Confuse them and you fix neither.

How this leak happens, step by step

  1. The file is assembled with every line the crew touched.
  2. Nobody checks each line against the order's rulebook — the unallowable $120 sails through.
  3. Nobody checks the proof — the $80 of dark, missing photos sails through too.
  4. The rulebook has its say at review, and both halves fall at once. Owner: the Processor, whose check should have caught both.

If you've done this work before

The $80 half is the one that stings in real life, because the work was real and the crew really did it. Teach the sentence that prevents it: proof is part of the work, not paperwork after the work. A job photographed badly is a job half done.

The line to remember: “Work without proof is work the rulebook cannot pay for.”

The proof — the split, as taught

$120Unallowable — outside the rulebook, e.g. personal items the order never listed
$80Unprovable — photos missing or too dark and blurry to read
$200Total first-step leak · Owner: the Processor

If this is all new to you

Every property carries an allowance — a ceiling, the highest amount the rulebook will pay for that property's work. Work priced above it is called over-allowable. It is not forbidden — but it needs a special approval before anyone does the work. A small worked example, synthetic: allowed work priced at $120 against an allowance of $100. That extra $20 is over-allowable, and it lives or dies on asking first.

How the approval is asked, step by step

  1. Spot that the bid passes the property's allowance — before dispatch, not after.
  2. Ask through the claim portal — the system where claims are filed.
  3. Ask in time: at least five business days before the conveyance due date (conveyance is the day the house is handed to the agency that insures the loan).
  4. Only do the over-allowable work once the approval lands. In our story, nobody asked — so the client cut the $100. Owner: the Vendor Manager's bid/approval step.

If you've done this work before

One caution to say out loud every time: portals and schedules change. The five-business-day timing and the portal route must be verified as current before anyone treats them as today's fact — the programme flags this item “verify before teaching,” and the honest teacher says so.

The line to remember: “Over-allowable is not forbidden. Unasked is.”

The proof — and its honest limit

The $120-against-$100 example and the $100 cut are Session 9's synthetic worked numbers. The portal timing carries the session's own warning: verify the current schedule before teaching it as current, because dates and portals change.

Chapter 5 · Leaks three and four

One step held at zero. Then $150 fell at the door.

Approved $700, invoiced $700 — zero leaked, because on these orders gross equals net: there is no client discount to deduct, so the approved amount is invoiced in full. Then, at Paid, $150 fell: $60 a rejection nobody fixed, $50 short-paid, $40 a property adjustment.

Celebrate the zero. It means the invoice matched the approval exactly — and it only happens when the desk before it did its job.

Say it in class

“A seven-hundred-dollar approval invoices at seven hundred dollars — not seven hundred minus something. But always check the order, because discount rules differ by client.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

In much of business, the amount approved and the amount billed differ because a discount or fee is taken out in between. On these orders, that middle bite does not exist: approved $700 means invoice $700, in full. The skill is not memorising “no discount” — it is knowing the rule belongs to this order and checking the next one fresh.

How the zero is earned, step by step

  1. The approval lands at $700.
  2. The invoice is built from the approval — completion quantities only, bid and price columns untouched.
  3. The numbers match exactly, so nothing falls between Approved and Invoiced.
  4. That is the whole trick: the zero is manufactured upstream, by accuracy.

If you've done this work before

Say the warning every single time, because trainees love a universal rule: discount rules differ by client, and this one is order-specific. What is true on this order may not be true on the next one — check the order.

The line to remember: “Gross equals net — on this order. Check the next one.”

The proof — provenance, stated plainly

Gross-equals-net is one of the programme's standing rules for these orders, listed in the blueprint's standing rules — an operating rule, taught with its order-specific warning attached, exactly as Session 9 states it.

If this is all new to you

$60 — a rejection nobody fixed. A rejection is the client sending the file back saying something is wrong. It is not the end; it is a task. The only answer is to fix it with evidence and send it again — never to argue without proof. $50 — short-paid: paid below the invoice, for a quantity the client did not accept. $40 — a property adjustment: money moved on the same property to cover another loss there — a whole story of its own, coming on Slide 10.

How the last leak happens, step by step

  1. The invoice goes out correct — $700.
  2. A rejection comes back and sits unfixed: −$60.
  3. A quantity is not accepted and the payment comes in short: −$50.
  4. An adjustment is booked against the property: −$40. Paid lands at $550. Owner of this ground: the Client Manager.

If you've done this work before

Notice the pattern across all three: none of them is a field problem. The house was fine. The last leak is an office-and-follow-through leak — files not chased, fixes not sent, matches not made. That is why the Client Manager's desk exists, and why Slide 8 gives it a full chapter.

The line to remember: “The only answer to a rejection is evidence, sent again.”

The proof — the split, as taught

$60Rejection — sent back, never fixed
$50Short-paid — below invoice on an unaccepted quantity
$40Property adjustment — moved on the same property (Slide 10)
Chapter 6 · Three people, one file — first desk

First desk: the Vendor Manager.

Orders arrive in the morning, and the Vendor Manager reads each one like a pilot reads a checklist: scope, then rulebook. First question is always permission. If the house might still be occupied — if the signs are unclear — the answer is HOLD: do not start, and escalate the question to someone who can decide it. No exceptions.

Only when permission is clear does anyone get sent anywhere. A fast dispatch to a house you may not enter is not fast. It is wrong.

Say it in class

“The Vendor Manager gets the right crew to the right house — with permission.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

After permission comes the pick: the crew needs the right skill for this job, they need to work in this area, and they need to be free on this day. Then the dispatch — the sending-out — carries three things exactly: the scope of work, the deadline, and the lockbox code exactly as the order states it. A lockbox is the small locked box on the house that holds the key; its code must match the order digit for digit. The Vendor Manager then confirms the crew accepted, tracks the visit while it happens, collects the photos and report, checks the file is complete — and only then hands it to the Processor.

How one order moves, step by step

  1. Read scope, then rulebook. Ask permission first — unclear occupancy means HOLD and escalate.
  2. Pick the crew on skill, area, availability.
  3. Dispatch scope, lockbox code digit-for-digit, deadline. Confirm acceptance.
  4. Track the visit. Collect photos and report. Check completeness.
  5. Hand a complete file to the Processor — never a mess for the next person to inherit.

If you've done this work before

The complexity is the count of moving parts: many orders, many places, different time zones, weather that ruins a day, houses that will not open, crews that do not show. Name that honestly in class — trainees who expect a tidy queue quit at the first rainy Monday; trainees told the truth plan backups.

The line to remember: “Permission first, then the right crew — never the other way round.”

The proof — the breaks, named in advance

Session 9 names this desk's failure modes so the class can recognise them: the wrong crew sent to the wrong job; a visit missed entirely; a no-show with no backup crew ready; and the worst one — an incomplete handoff to the Processor, photos and report unchecked or missing, so the next person inherits a mess.

If this is all new to you

Signs a house might still be lived in are not always clear-cut: lights, a car, curtains, a neighbour's word. The rule does not ask you to be certain — it asks the opposite. If the signs are unclear, you hold. Escalate means send the question up to someone who can decide it. Entering a home someone still lives in is the one error this industry cannot take back, so the rule is built to over-stop rather than under-stop.

How HOLD works, step by step

  1. Read the order; check the occupancy signs in the file.
  2. Clear permission? Proceed to the pick. Unclear? Stop here.
  3. Mark HOLD, escalate with what you saw, and wait for a decision.
  4. No deadline, however loud, outranks this step. No exceptions — the session's own words.

If you've done this work before

Praise a held order in class the way you would praise a caught error. Crews and managers alike read HOLD as failure unless the teacher reframes it: a hold is the permission system succeeding at exactly the moment it was designed for.

The line to remember: “If the signs are unclear, the answer is HOLD. No exceptions.”

The proof — where this rule sits

The permission-first rule opens the Vendor Manager's chapter in Session 9 and is stated there without qualification. It connects back to the chain on the wall — Bank → Servicer → National → Our office → Field crew: permission travels down the same chain the order does.

Chapter 7 · Three people, one file — second desk

Second desk: the Processor.

The photos and the report land here, and this desk turns proof into a clean, honest invoice: every photo tagged to its line item and flagged Before, During, or After, date-stamps checked, quantities honest, allowability checked — and if there are gaps, the file goes back to the field. Gaps are never papered over.

This desk prepares the file up to ready — and stops there. Ready For Office is the owner's mark. The Processor never marks it.

Say it in class

“A missing photo is fixed by taking the photo — not by writing around it.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

First, the photos go into the office engine — the office's own system, not a client portal, and never confused with one. Each photo is tagged to its line item — tied to the exact job it proves — and flagged Before, During, or After, so the proof chain reads like a story: how the house looked, what happened, how it ended. Then the date-stamp check: a date-stamp is the date printed on the photo itself; some rulebooks require it, others do not — so check the order, and if it is unclear, the safe move is to date-stamp anyway. Then honest quantities, checked by hand. Then allowability against the rulebook. Then the invoice — built by entering completion quantities only, how much work was actually completed, never altering the bid or price columns. Then quality control: every photo clear, right place, right time, right scope, nothing missing.

How one file is processed, step by step

  1. Photos into the office engine; tag each to its line item; flag Before / During / After.
  2. Date-stamp check against this order; unclear means stamp it anyway.
  3. Quantities by hand — cubic-yard maths, counts, measurements.
  4. Allowability: is every line something this rulebook allows?
  5. Build the invoice on completion quantities only. QC the whole file. Gaps? Back to the field.

If you've done this work before

The volume is the complexity here: so many photos, tagging that must be exact, quantities that get disputed, items the rulebook will not allow, missing date-stamps, invoice maths, different formats for different clients, and rework loops when files come back. The named breaks: bad photos, wrong quantities, unallowable items, missing date-stamps, evidence nobody tagged.

The line to remember: “Turn proof into a clean, honest invoice — or send it back.”

The proof — one piece of maths the class must own

The cubic-yard check from Class 8 lives on this desk: length × width × height in feet, divided by 27. A pile 9 ft × 6 ft × 3 ft is 162 cubic feet = 6 cubic yards. Bill it as 10 and the maths fails in front of anyone who checks — the decision slide at the end of this class turns on exactly this.

If this is all new to you

Ready For Office — RFO — is the stamp that says “this file is ready for the office to send on.” It looks like a small button. It is actually a promise: someone senior has taken responsibility for this file. That is why the mark belongs to the owner alone. Preparing a file beautifully and then stopping one step short is not unfinished work — it is the job, done exactly as designed.

How the line works, step by step

  1. Processor finishes every check and builds the invoice.
  2. File sits at ready — complete, honest, waiting.
  3. The owner cross-checks it himself and marks RFO himself.
  4. Only then does the file move to submission — and submission itself waits for the owner's word (Slide 12 tells that sequence in full).

If you've done this work before

Say this slowly in class, because it is the moral centre of the whole job: the person who prepares the file is never the person who approves its readiness. Two pairs of eyes, two different duties. If a trainee ever feels pressure to “just mark it,” this slide is the answer they were given in training.

The line to remember: “Prepare it up to ready — and stop there. RFO is the owner's mark.”

The proof — provenance, stated plainly

The RFO rule is one of the programme's standing rules, listed in the blueprint: the owner marks Ready For Office himself; the Processor prepares and stops. Taught here as an operating rule of this work.

Chapter 8 · Three people, one file — third desk

Third desk: the Client Manager.

The prepared file leaves the office and is submitted in the client portal — the client's own system, never the office engine. Then this desk tracks the review, fixes rejections with evidence and resubmits, waits out the lag — about sixty days — and matches every payment back to its invoice.

Say the difference out loud one more time: office engine is ours, client portal is theirs. Confusing the two is how files get lost.

Say it in class

“A payment younger than sixty days is not late. It is lag — the normal travel time of money. Tracking, not panic, is the job.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Submission is not the finish line; it is the start of a watch. The client reviews. Sometimes the file comes back — a rejection — and each one is a specific complaint with a specific fix: find the evidence, attach it, resubmit. Then the waiting, which has a number: about sixty days for payment to travel. Delinquency would mean someone failed to pay; lag just means the money is on its normal road. This desk's craft is telling those two apart without flinching.

How one file is carried, step by step

  1. Submit the prepared file in the client portal — the client's system.
  2. Track the review. Log every rejection the day it lands.
  3. Fix each rejection with evidence; resubmit; track again.
  4. Wait the ~60 days as lag, not lateness — track, don't panic.
  5. Match the payment to the invoice when it arrives — by address (next slide shows why).

If you've done this work before

The sixty-day rule protects two things at once: the client relationship (no chasing money that is simply travelling) and the office's honesty (no calling lag “income” before it lands, and no calling it “lost” before its time). Age every due against the sixty-day cycle, never against hope.

The line to remember: “Tracking, not panic, is the job during those sixty days.”

The proof — provenance, stated plainly

The ~60-day payment cycle is one of the programme's standing rules: dues younger than about sixty days are expected lag, not delinquency. Losses and collection pressure are read against that cycle, as Session 9 teaches.

If this is all new to you

Think of two buildings. In our building, we prepare: photos tagged, quantities checked, invoice built. In their building, we submit and the client decides. A file “sent” in the wrong building was never sent at all — it was filed in our own drawer and called done. That single confusion explains a surprising share of “the client never paid us” stories.

How to keep them apart, step by step

  1. Ask, before touching anything: whose system is this — ours or the client's?
  2. Preparation happens only in the office engine.
  3. Submission happens only in the client portal.
  4. When handing over, say which system the file is in — out loud, every time.

If you've done this work before

Make the class say the difference out loud, together — the session insists on it, because this is the confusion that loses files. It feels theatrical for five seconds and saves months later.

The line to remember: “The office engine is not a client portal. Never mix the two.”

The proof — where this rule sits

Portal separation is a blueprint standing rule, repeated at both the Processor's desk (photos go into the office engine) and this desk (submission goes into the client portal). Two mentions, one rule, no exceptions in the session.

Chapter 9 · The detective work

Order A shows no payment. Is it unpaid?

Not until you check the chain. Clients do not always answer the way you expect: sometimes a submitted order is answered by a follow-up order — a different order at the same property — and the payment arrives under the new one. Order A is not unpaid. Order A is superseded: replaced by the newer order.

Match by address, not by number. Numbers differ across systems. The address is the key that proves it is the same house.

Check the chain yourself

Our house's file: Order A was submitted and shows no payment at all. Weeks later, Order B appears at the same address — and payment arrives under Order B. Before you touch the verdict, tap what you would check first.

Say it in class

“Never call an order unpaid until you have checked the chain. Match by address, not by number.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Work through it slowly. Order A goes in at our house. Nothing comes back under A — the payment column stays empty, week after week. The lazy reading is “unpaid.” The careful reading starts with a question: did the client answer A with something else? They did — Order B, a follow-up at the same address, carrying the payment. A and B are the same job wearing two numbers, because the same job can carry one number in the office engine and another in the client portal.

How a chain check runs, step by step

  1. An order shows no payment past its expected lag.
  2. Before any “unpaid” label: search the property by its full address.
  3. Look for a follow-up order at that address — different number, same house.
  4. If payment sits under the follow-up, mark the old order superseded / CHAIN-PAID — not unpaid.
  5. Only when the address check finds nothing does the loss investigation begin (next slide).

If you've done this work before

This is the rule that keeps loss reports honest: a WO-number search that finds nothing proves nothing, because numbers differ per system. The address-first check is slower by minutes and saves whole properties from being written off while their money sits one order over.

The line to remember: “Superseded, not unpaid — until the address says otherwise.”

The proof — where this rule sits

The chain story and the address rule are Session 9's own, told as the Client Manager's detective work: follow-up orders at the same property, payment under the new number, matching by address because numbers differ across systems. The worked example is synthetic and labelled in the session.

If this is all new to you

A house has one address and can collect many order numbers over its life — one per system, sometimes one per follow-up. If you file houses by number, one house becomes three ghosts. If you file by address, the ghosts collapse back into one house with a history — and its money can be followed from order to order.

How the key is used, step by step

  1. Every match starts from the property address, written in full.
  2. Order numbers are recorded as attributes of that address — per system.
  3. A new number at a known address triggers a chain check, not a new file.
  4. Payments, losses, and adjustments are all reconciled at the address.

If you've done this work before

Hold this for the next slide: the property-level adjustment — money received but not spent, set against the same property's loss — is only findable because matching is by address. Number-first books make that money invisible.

The line to remember: “The address is the key. Numbers are just labels systems stick on her.”

The proof — the chain on the wall, again

Bank → Servicer → National → Our office → Field crew. An order travels all five links, and each link's system may number it differently. The one thing no link changes is where the house stands — which is exactly why the address, not the number, is the matching key.

Chapter 10 · Losses, honestly

Every loss gets a reason. No exceptions, no blanks.

A loss is money that was invoiced and did not come back. Its reason lives in a hard-to-find place — on the order's invoice part, beside the payment amounts — and every loss gets exactly one of six reason codes. The sixth, UNEXPLAINED, is not an answer. It is a queue, driven to zero.

REJECTEDRejected — and never fixed
SHORT-PAIDPaid below the invoice
UNALLOWABLEThe scope sat outside the rulebook
ADJUSTEDAbsorbed by a property-level adjustment
CHAIN-PAIDPaid under a follow-up order at the same property
UNEXPLAINEDNo reason found yet — a queue, never a final answer

Try the adjustment yourself

The story, synthetic and in round numbers: on one property, $500 arrived with no cost recorded against it — money received but not spent. That same property carries a $300 loss. Change the two numbers and watch what the adjustment leaves behind.

And who approves it? The owner approves the adjustment before it is booked — nobody books an adjustment on their own authority. How is it found? By matching receipts to the property by address. Always the address.

Say it in class

“Every loss gets a reason. UNEXPLAINED is a queue, never an answer.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

A reason code is a one-word verdict on why money did not come back — and it is only earned by looking. The reason is found on the order's invoice part, beside the payment amounts, a place that is genuinely hard to find; that is why this is a taught skill and not common sense. A loss counts as “no reason” only after that invoice part has actually been checked. Three synthetic examples to anchor the codes: rejected for a missing date-stamp → REJECTED if never fixed; short-paid after an over-allowable piece went in without approval → SHORT-PAID; an unallowable removal of personal property the order never covered → UNALLOWABLE.

How a loss gets its reason, step by step

  1. Open the order's invoice part — beside the payment amounts.
  2. Read what actually happened to the money there.
  3. Run the chain check by address before choosing any code.
  4. Assign exactly one code. If nothing is found, it enters the UNEXPLAINED queue — listed by property, reason field blank, reviewed weekly.

If you've done this work before

The Client Manager owns the unexplained queue. “Zero” does not mean the losses vanished — it means no blank reason fields remain: every loss has a reason, or an owner chasing one. Teach that definition of zero carefully; it is the difference between a clean book and a swept floor.

The line to remember: “Zero unexplained means every loss has a reason — not that every loss came back.”

The proof — the six codes, as taught

REJECTED · SHORT-PAID · UNALLOWABLE · ADJUSTED · CHAIN-PAID · UNEXPLAINED — Session 9's code list, verbatim, with the weekly-review discipline for the queue: listed by property, reviewed weekly, driven to zero.

If this is all new to you

Sometimes a property ends up holding money: payment arrived, but no cost was ever recorded against it — no crew paid, nothing spent. Left alone, that balance just sits there, unmatched, while the same property shows a loss somewhere else. The adjustment is the honest meeting of the two: take $300 of the received $500 and set it against the $300 loss. What remains — $200 received-but-unspent — still has to be reconciled. Nothing disappears; it is accounted for.

How an adjustment is done, step by step

  1. Match receipts to the property — by address, always.
  2. Find received money with no cost recorded against it on that property.
  3. Find that same property's losses or shortfalls.
  4. Propose the offset — then stop. The owner approves before anything is booked.
  5. Book it as ADJUSTED, and carry any remainder as still-to-reconcile.

If you've done this work before

The approval gate is the lesson inside the lesson. An adjustment rewrites what a property's book says, so it is never a solo act — the person who finds the balance is never the person who approves booking it. Same shape as RFO: prepare, then the owner decides.

The line to remember: “Found by address, approved by the owner, booked as ADJUSTED.”

The proof — the numbers, as taught

$500Received on the property, no cost recorded
− $300Set against the same property's loss
$200Received-but-unspent, still to reconcile

Synthetic worked example from Session 9, in round numbers so the class can follow it on their fingers. Try your own numbers in the calculator above the notes.

Chapter 11 · Your verdict

Approve, fix, or hold? Name the rung and the owner.

One synthetic invoice, $400. Grass cut, $60 — photos good. Secure, $150 — but the photo of one lock is missing. Debris, $150 — billed as 10 cubic yards, though the pile measures 9 × 6 × 3 feet: 162 cubic feet ÷ 27 = 6 cubic yards. And $40 for hauling away a television the order never listed. Pairs argue, then vote.

Give your verdict first

Tap your verdict — then read the expert's, and check whether you named the same rung and the same owner.

Say it in class

“Do not approve a file with an unallowable line, wrong maths, and a missing photo — and do not reject it outright either, because everything here is fixable with evidence.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Take the invoice line by line. Grass $60: clean — photos good, nothing to fix. Secure $150: the work may be fine, but one lock's photo is missing, so that part is unprovable as it stands — the photo must be taken properly, in the field. Debris $150: the pile is 6 cubic yards, billed as 10 — the quantity is wrong, so the line must be corrected to the honest measure. Television $40: the order never listed it — unallowable, so the line comes out entirely. Three fixes, three different kinds: prove it, measure it, remove it.

How the verdict is reached, step by step

  1. Check every line against the rulebook — the TV line fails allowability.
  2. Check every quantity by hand — 162 ÷ 27 = 6, not 10.
  3. Check every proof — one lock photo is missing.
  4. Verdict: FIX, not approve (three faults) and not hold/reject (all three are fixable with evidence).
  5. Rung: Allowable. Owner: the Processor. The Client Manager holds submission until the fix lands.

If you've done this work before

The rubric is the session's own: a verdict alone earns nothing — the trainee must name the rung and the owner with it. “Fix it” without “Allowable, Processor” is a guess wearing a uniform. And notice: this one small invoice contains the whole class — an unallowable line, a quantity error, and a proof gap, the three leaks of the first staircase step in miniature.

The line to remember: “Verdict, rung, owner — all three, every time.”

The proof — the invoice, as set

LineBilledFinding
Grass cut$60Photos good — clean
Secure$150One lock photo missing — back to the field
Debris$150Billed 10 CY; measures 9×6×3 ft = 6 CY — correct it
TV haul-away$40Never listed on the order — unallowable, remove it
Total claimed$400Verdict: FIX · Rung: Allowable · Owner: Processor

If this is all new to you

Approve would send all three faults to the client, where each becomes a leak you have already met: the TV line falls as unallowable, the debris line falls on its maths, the secure line falls for missing proof. Hold — rejecting the whole file — throws away a clean grass line and real secure and debris work that only needs correcting. Fix is the verdict that respects both the rulebook and the work: nothing false goes out, nothing true is wasted.

How to judge any file this way, step by step

  1. Any fault that evidence can cure? Then it is not a hold.
  2. Any fault still in the file? Then it is not an approve.
  3. What remains is FIX — with each fault named, its fix named, and its owner named.

If you've done this work before

Grade the reasoning, not the tap. A pair that votes FIX but cannot say why the maths fails has guessed kindly. A pair that votes HOLD and defends it with “nothing unprovable should travel” has reasoned — correct the verdict, praise the spine, and show them the fixable-with-evidence test.

The line to remember: “Fixable with evidence means FIX — never papered over, never thrown away.”

The proof — the decision's place in the session

This is Session 9's scripted decision moment: one synthetic invoice, verdict approve / fix / hold, rung and owner named aloud. The expert verdict, fixes, and the Client Manager's submission hold are the session's own.

Chapter 12 · The handoff

Three people. One file. One promise about how it travels.

Walk the submission sequence out loud, in full, because this sequence is a promise the class must never shorten: complete the work — report the finished state — the owner cross-checks it himself — submit only on the owner's word. Then the whole class says the handoff line together, one role at a time.

Next class, she is judged — the exam of her whole story. Bring the staircase with you. You will need every step.

Say it in class — the whole class, one role at a time

“The Vendor Manager gets the right crew to the right house with permission. The Processor turns proof into a clean, honest invoice. The Client Manager turns the invoice into cash — and explains every dollar that did not come back.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Four beats, and the order is the meaning. The work is completed first — really completed, in the field. Then the finished state is reported — honestly, gaps included. Then the owner cross-checks it himself — his eyes, not a summary of someone else's. Only then, on his word, is anything submitted. Skip the third beat and the office is submitting on trust; skip the fourth and it is submitting on habit. Both are how bad files travel.

How the sequence runs, step by step

  1. Complete the work.
  2. Report the finished state.
  3. The owner cross-checks everything himself.
  4. Submit — only on the owner's word, after his cross-check.

If you've done this work before

This sequence is the same shape as everything else today: RFO belongs to the owner, adjustments are approved by the owner, submission waits for the owner's word. One principle in three costumes — preparation is shared, the final call is not.

The line to remember: “Complete, report, cross-check, submit — in that order, on his word.”

The proof — provenance, stated plainly

The submission sequence is a programme standing rule, stated in Session 9 as the promise the class must never shorten, and in the blueprint's standing rules alongside the RFO rule.

If this is all new to you

If you remember nothing else, remember the shape: money walks down five steps and leaks at four of them; three people each guard part of the staircase; every dollar that still goes missing gets a one-word reason; and nothing travels to the client until the owner has checked it and said the word. That shape will organise every file you ever touch.

How to close the class, step by step

  1. Say the ladder once more, together: 1,000, 800, 700, 700, 550.
  2. Say the handoff line together, one role at a time (above).
  3. One line each, from memory: name one leak and its owner.
  4. Point forward: Class 10 judges the whole story — bring the staircase.

If you've done this work before

The retrieval to listen for is ownership, not arithmetic. Anyone can memorise 550. The trainee who says “the $80 was unprovable work, and it belonged to the Processor's check” has understood the job — that sentence is the class working.

The line to remember: “Explain every dollar that did not come back.”

The proof — the SAY lines, gathered

Open“Work done is not money earned. Money has to travel — and it leaks at every step.”
Rulebook“The rulebook on the order is the boss. If the rulebook does not allow it, we do not bill it.”
Proof“A gap in proof is not a small thing. A gap sends the file back to the field — never paper it over.”
Chain“Never call an order unpaid until you have checked the chain. Match by address, not by number.”
Losses“Every loss gets a reason. UNEXPLAINED is a queue, never an answer.”

Session 9's exact SAY lines, gathered from its chapters — the class's spoken spine, start to finish.

All 12 slides

The full arc of Class 9 on one screen — the staircase, the three desks, the chain, the six codes, and the verdict. Tap any slide to jump to it.

The logic behind this page

Why Class 9 is built the way it is, what its numbers are — and what they are not. One teacher to another, before the class walks in.

One staircase carries the whole session

Money is abstract until it has stairs to fall down. This page gives the class a single synthetic invoice — $1,000 claimed, $550 paid — and never lets go of it: every role, rule, and code in the session is introduced as the guard of one of its steps. By the decision slide, the trainees are not recalling five separate lessons; they are reading one staircase they have already walked four times.

Every number here is synthetic — on purpose, and labelled

  • No real amounts appear anywhere. The $1,000 ladder, the $400 decision invoice, the $500/$300 adjustment — all are the programme's made-up teaching figures, in round numbers, labelled synthetic on the slides themselves.
  • The ladder is not the contractor-chain funnel. Earlier sessions use a $100 → $55 chain illustration; Session 9's staircase is a different device (claimed-to-paid on one invoice), and Slide 3's notes say so explicitly so the two are never merged.
  • Round numbers are a teaching choice, so the class can follow leaks on their fingers and spend their attention on ownership, not arithmetic.

Rules are taught as standing rules, not as history

  • The rulebook-on-the-order rule, gross-equals-net on these orders, the ~60-day lag, RFO-by-the-owner, portal separation, address-first matching, and the submission sequence are this operation's standing rules — the drawers say so wherever they appear, rather than dressing them as research findings.
  • Gross-equals-net always travels with its warning: discount rules differ by client; check the order. The page never states it as a universal law.
  • Verify-current items are flagged, not hidden: the claim-portal route and the five-business-day over-allowable timing carry the session's own “verify as current before teaching” caution, printed in Slide 4's drawer.

Why the verdict is practised, not announced

  • The $400 invoice contains the whole class in miniature — an unallowable line, a quantity error (9×6×3 ft = 6 CY, billed as 10), and a proof gap — so the decision tests transfer, not memory.
  • The rubric grades the full sentence: verdict + rung + owner. “Fix” alone is a guess; “FIX, Allowable, Processor” is the skill.
  • Both wrong verdicts are instructive: approve ships the faults as leaks; hold wastes fixable work. The exercise copy walks trainees through both before revealing the expert line.

Running the class from this page

  • Open with guesses. Slide 1's question only works if the class hunts before you hand them the sentence.
  • Walk the staircase twice. Once on Slide 3, once from memory at the close — the second walk is the retrieval that makes it stick.
  • Say the system difference out loud, together, on Slide 8 — office engine vs client portal. It feels theatrical; it prevents lost files.
  • Protect the decision. If time runs short, cut discussion elsewhere — never the verdict on Slide 11.
  • Nothing here is real client data — the house is a teaching character, every invoice is synthetic, and no client, work-order number, address, or crew name appears anywhere.

Where it all came from

Every figure and rule on the slides names its home in its drawer. In short:

  • Session 9 of the programme — “Follow the Money: Three People, One Invoice” (storytelling telling and blueprint Session 9): the ladder and its leak splits, the bid formula, the three desks and their breaks, the chain story, the six reason codes, the adjustment example, the $400 decision invoice, and all SAY lines.
  • The blueprint's standing rules: rulebook-on-the-order, RFO-by-the-owner, ~60-day lag, gross-equals-net on these orders, office-engine / client-portal separation, address-first matching, and the submission sequence.
  • Class 8, carried forward: identify–document–quantify and the cubic-yard maths (9×6×3 ft = 162 cu ft ÷ 27 = 6 CY).

This is the demo version of Class 9 from the preservation training programme — shared so the teacher can look it over before the full class is built. Our house is a teaching character, made up for the story; the pictures are illustrations, not a real property. Every invoice, amount, and example in this class is synthetic — made up for teaching — and no real clients, work orders, addresses, or company details appear anywhere on the page.
